topic: claude vs chatgpt personal finance features
headline_marked: [[Claude Personal Finance offers default privacy]] vs. ChatGPT's Finances, both link to your bank
headline: Claude Personal Finance offers default privacy vs. ChatGPT's Finances, both link to your bank
summary: Anthropic's Claude Personal Finance and OpenAI's ChatGPT Finances both offer bank account insights, but Claude defaults to not using your data for training, unlike ChatGPT.
details: Anthropic's new Personal Finance feature for Claude rivals OpenAI's ChatGPT Finances, both aiming to help users understand their money. While neither offers expert financial advice, their approaches to privacy and data handling set them apart.

Both AI chatbots cover a broad spectrum of personal finance, answering questions about financial goals like buying a house or creating savings plans. They can also generate visual dashboards for expenses, investments, and spending habits.

To activate, users must link their bank accounts via Plaid, connecting to major institutions like Bank of America or Chase. Both tools gain "read-only" access, meaning they can view information but cannot make any changes to accounts.

Anthropic specifies Claude can see bank and account names, type, last four digits, balances, credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. OpenAI's Finances tool similarly accesses balances, transactions, investments, and liabilities.

The key difference lies in privacy settings: Claude's Personal Finance conversations are not used for model training by default. Unlinking an account also removes previously provided data from Claude's view.

In contrast, ChatGPT's Finances conversations follow general model training settings, which are on by default. Users must manually opt out in settings to prevent their data from being used to improve the model.

Anthropic further differentiates Claude's feature by stating it has no ads or sponsored recommendations, nor does it offer its own credit cards, loans, or savings accounts. OpenAI has been testing ads for cheaper ChatGPT tiers.

OpenAI plans to expand ChatGPT's Finances with Intuit partnerships for credit card applications and tax questions. Anthropic seeks input from financial institutions to enhance Claude's Personal Finance tool.

topic: gpu supply problem no end in sight
headline_marked: [[GPU supply problem has no end in sight]], with prices expected to rise 400% by 2026
headline: GPU supply problem has no end in sight, with prices expected to rise 400% by 2026
summary: AI data centers are consuming memory as fast as it's made, driving 'chipflation' with DRAM prices projected to climb 400% by 2026 and consumer GPU costs skyrocketing.
details: AI data centers are rapidly consuming memory, leading to a significant GPU supply problem and "chipflation" across the consumer tech industry. JP Morgan reports that dynamic random access memory (DRAM) prices are expected to rise by 400 percent by the end of 2026 compared to 2024 levels.

This shortage has caused consumer GPU prices to vastly outpace general inflation. For example, Nvidia's GeForce RTX 5090, launched in January 2025 with a suggested price of $1,999, currently retails for $4,920 above that MSRP. Foreign markets are also seeing significant price increases.

The ripple effect extends to the broader consumer electronics market. The Consumer Price Index for software and accessories has increased by nearly a quarter over the last two years, and reports indicate rises in video game console and laptop prices, leading to a fall in PC shipments. Resellers are capitalizing, with PlayStation 5 Pro units selling for roughly $500 above MSRP.

The crisis is projected to continue well into the 2030s, with many chip producers already having sold much of their 2027 supplies. Some are now focusing sales on 2028 and beyond, indicating a long-term imbalance.

At its core, the GPU shortage is a memory problem, specifically driven by the demand for High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). AI developers require vast stores of HBM chips to train and run their models, causing demand to far outpace current market supplies.

HBM competes for the same wafer capacity as traditional DRAM and other memory products. Suppliers are reorienting production towards advanced HBM chips due to high demand and better profit margins, selling HBM for about 30 percent more than standard DRAM. This shift is further complicated by the transition to newer HBM generations like HBM4 and HBM4E.

HBM is projected to account for nearly 30 percent of total DRAM production in 2027, up from 20 percent the year before, potentially reaching almost 40 percent by 2029. More broadly, AI data centers are expected to consume approximately 70 percent of global DRAM supplies this year.

The market is highly concentrated, with Micron Technologies, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix accounting for about 90 percent of global DRAM production. These three companies are expanding capacity but continue to prioritize data centers over consumer GPUs, exacerbating the shortage for consumers.

Industry leaders are expressing serious concerns, with Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra expecting supply to be "much tighter in calendar 2027 and 2028." SK Hynix's chairman Chey Tae-won stated it will take "at least four to five years" to build adequate wafer supply, with production lagging 20 percent behind demand until at least 2030.

Major suppliers have already pre-sold significant portions of their future production capacity. Micron, for instance, has reportedly sold 75 percent of its 2027 HBM output, securing sales at favorable terms.
